turn_text: With regard to the transportation and infrastructure committee, what is ahead for you and what are the heavy lifting tasks that are really on the table?

We have a lot of heavy lifting. And as I said, when I was characterizing serving on the AG Committee, I think also a highlight for me is that I do serve on the Transportation Infrastructure Committee. It too is a committee where you can't apply partisan labels to what we're trying to get accomplished here. We need a long-term highway bill. What we voted on back in May was a two-month extension to keep that funded just through the end of this month. And so when we're talking about a sense of urgency, that applies to the highway bill as well. Here's what I support. There's a piece of legislation that has bipartisan support at this point that calls for the corporate profits that now sit overseas to the tune of $2.1 trillion. I support a move that would bring those profits home through something that's called repatriation. That would give us about six years worth of funding for to address our infrastructure needs. Now, there are actually three different versions of this repatriation that are all financed at different rates. The bill that I support, and maybe this gets a little too technical, but the reason I'm bringing it up is that it has bipartisan support. There's a president's version of this. There's a more strictly Republican version, and there's a bipartisan version. of this. I support the bipartisan version that taxes that at 8.75%. That is at a rate that corporations can bring that home and it can give us adequate funding. Now that is what I support. The reality is I don't think that's going to come up for a vote here before the Highway Trust Fund is empty at the end of this month. So what I would anticipate happening is that we would probably have another extension. I think it's a terrible way to do business. It doesn't give our road builders and our construction workers and our engineers and our state governments the time that they need to plan for long-term infrastructure projects. But it's an unfortunate reality of Washington DC that we keep putting these measures on the table that all they do is kick the problem down the road. And we're not coming up with these long-term solutions. The other part of this bill that I support, Jeff, it calls also for a study to look at long-term sustainable funding for our infrastructure needs. Now, we're a country that a huge competitive advantage that we've had globally for generations has been that we've got an infrastructure system where we can move our goods in an efficient manner. But what's been happening Really, I would argue for close to the last 10 plus years is that we haven't addressed our infrastructure needs. We've seen devastating effects as a result of that with the bridge that collapsed in Minneapolis. We've got a situation, if you just want to even look at the state of Illinois, that I represent one of 18 congressional districts in Illinois. We've got close to 27,000 bridges in our state, and more than 2,200 of those are considered structurally deficient. And that just means that we haven't kept pace with the steel work on it, with the concrete work on it. And then there's another, almost 2,000 that were built, that they're not sufficiently handled now. So, you know, this is a big problem. That's just the bridges alone, and then we've got, you know, we've got about 15% of our highways aren't keeping pace with what our needs are now, too. So a lot of needs out there, and that's just the upkeep that we're talking about, let alone addressing our future needs.
